rulers.title: Where the three rulers come from
rulers.mini: Three ways to measure between two coordinates: an arc on a globe, a straight line on a latitude-longitude grid, a straight line on the polar flat-earth disc. Only one can match what travellers log.
rulers.text: Give two places by their latitude and longitude and ask how far apart they are. A globe answers with an arc: the central angle between them times the radius. A flat map answers with a ruler, and the answer depends on which map: on a latitude-longitude grid, Pythagoras on the two differences; on the polar disc that flat-earth maps use, the law of cosines on the triangle with the North Pole [1]. The same coordinates, three geometries, three distances. Ships, aircraft and odometers log only one of them. The drawings are schematics of the algebra, not to scale.
rulers.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: logged travel distances that match one of the flat rulers everywhere, not the arc.
three.title: Same endpoints, three measurements
three.mini: The same two endpoints, measured three ways: an arc on the globe, a straight line on a latitude-longitude grid, a straight chord on the polar disc. They agree only in special cases.
three.text: The same pair of endpoints, measured by each model in its own geometry: along the arc of a great circle on the globe, along a straight line on a latitude-longitude grid, and along a straight chord on the polar disc. The three numbers differ, and not by a constant factor: how much they differ depends on where the two points are and in which direction the segment runs. That is what makes the comparison testable. A flat map could always be rescaled to fix one distance; it cannot fix all of them at once. The drawing is schematic.
three.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: one flat ruler that matches measured distances in every direction and region.
arc.title: The globe's ruler: an arc
arc.mini: On a globe, the distance between two places is the radius times the central angle σ between them. Latitudes and the difference in longitude set σ; nothing else enters.
arc.text: On a globe the shortest path between two places is an arc of a great circle, and its length is R × σ, where σ is the angle between the two places at the Earth's centre. The latitudes of the two points and their difference in longitude set σ through one formula of spherical trigonometry, best written in its haversine form, which stays accurate for short distances [1]. The radius only scales the answer: for two pairs of places to be equally far apart on a globe, they need only the same central angle. The drawing is schematic.
arc.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: pairs with the same central angle measured at different distances.
grid.title: A flat ruler: the latitude-longitude grid
grid.mini: Lay latitude and longitude out as a square grid: x = Rλ, y = Rφ. The ruler is Pythagoras on the two differences. Correct along the equator and the meridians, it inflates every east-west leg away from the equator.
grid.text: The simplest flat map lays latitude and longitude out as a square grid, the equidistant cylindrical projection: a point's x is R times its longitude, its y is R times its latitude [1]. The ruler is Pythagoras on the two differences. It is right along the meridians and along the equator. Everywhere else it inflates east-west distances, by 1/cos φ at latitude φ: twice at 60°, without limit toward the poles. Its grid is symmetric across the equator, so it keeps mirror pairs equal while making both too long. The drawing is schematic.
grid.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: east-west legs at high latitude measured as long as this grid makes them.
disc.title: The flat-earth ruler: the polar disc
disc.mini: On the polar disc, a point's distance from the centre is R times its colatitude and its bearing is its longitude. The ruler is the law of cosines. Right from the North Pole outward, wrong everywhere else.
disc.text: The map most flat-earth arguments use is the north-polar azimuthal equidistant projection: the North Pole at the centre, each point at a distance from it equal to R times its colatitude (90° minus latitude), in the direction of its longitude [1]. The ruler between two points is the law of cosines on the triangle they make with the centre. Distances from the North Pole are exactly right. Every other distance is distorted, and more so the farther south: the southern hemisphere is stretched into a ring around the northern one. The drawing is schematic.
disc.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: southern distances as long as the disc draws them, logged by ships and aircraft.
mirror.title: Mirror latitudes, two different radii
mirror.mini: On a globe, the parallels at 45° N and 45° S are mirror images, the same size. On the polar disc they become two circles of very different radii, the southern one three times as long around.
mirror.text: Take the same latitude north and south of the equator. On a globe the two parallels are mirror images: the same circle, the same length. On the polar disc, a parallel is a circle around the North Pole of radius R times the colatitude, so 45° N becomes a circle of radius 45° of arc and 45° S one of 135°: three times the radius, three times the length. Every east-west journey in the south would be three times longer than its mirror in the north at that latitude. The drawing is schematic.
mirror.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: east-west journeys at 45° S measured three times longer than their mirrors at 45° N.
parallel.title: One parallel, two circumferences
parallel.mini: The same parallel of latitude: on a globe its radius is R cos φ, on the disc it is R times the colatitude. They agree only at the North Pole. At the equator the disc is already 57% too long.
parallel.text: Where a parallel of latitude φ sits decides the length of every east-west journey along it. On a globe it is a circle of radius R cos φ. On the polar disc it is a circle of radius R × (90° − φ), in radians. Their ratio, (π/2 − φ)/cos φ, does not depend on R at all. It equals 1 only at the North Pole, is 1.11 at 45° N, 1.57 at the equator, 3.33 at 45° S and 17 at 80° S. The disc never reads short and never reads true except at the pole. The drawing is schematic.
parallel.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: east-west distances along parallels that grow toward the south as the disc predicts.
stretch.title: How much the disc stretches, latitude by latitude
stretch.mini: The polar disc's east-west stretch against the globe: ×1 at the North Pole, ×1.57 at the equator, ×3.33 at 45° S, ×17 at 80° S. Vehicles log ×1 everywhere.
stretch.text: The factor by which the polar disc stretches an east-west distance compared with the globe, plotted by latitude: (π/2 − φ)/cos φ, with φ in radians. It is ×1 at the North Pole, ×1.11 at 45° N, ×1.57 at the equator, ×3.33 at 45° S and ×17.09 at 80° S [1]. The flat line at ×1 is what ships, aircraft and vehicles actually log. The curve does not depend on the size of the Earth: R cancels. A mirror pair of journeys at ±45° should differ by a factor of three on the disc; on the globe, and in practice, they are equal.
stretch.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: journeys at 45° S logged three times longer than their mirrors at 45° N.
legs.title: Two legs of exactly 60°
legs.mini: A leg over the North Pole (60° N 0° to 60° N 180°) and a leg along the equator (0° to 60° E) are both exactly 60° of arc on the globe: 6,672 km each. Any route planner returns both numbers.
legs.text: Two legs chosen so that the globe makes them equal to the kilometre. The polar leg runs from 60° N 0° to 60° N 180°: its great circle goes straight over the North Pole, 30° down each side. The equator leg runs from 0° 0° to 0° 60° E. Both subtend exactly 60° at the Earth's centre, so both measure 6,672 km. The equality is exact, not fitted, and does not even need the radius; any route planner returns both numbers [1]. The drawing shows each leg in its own plane.
legs.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the two legs logged at different lengths.
legs3.title: The same two legs under three rulers
legs3.mini: Two legs the globe makes equal, 6,672 km each. The latitude-longitude grid stretches the polar one to 20,015 km. The polar disc stretches the equator one to 10,008 km. Each flat map breaks a different leg.
legs3.text: The same two legs of 60° under three rulers. On the globe, each lies on its own great circle and both measure 6,672 km. On the latitude-longitude grid, the polar leg from 60° N 0° to 60° N 180° becomes a straight line along the 60° parallel of 20,015 km, while the equator leg stays right. On the polar disc, the polar leg stays right, 6,672 km through the centre, and the equator leg becomes a chord of 10,008 km. Neither flat map can hold the two equal, and they fail in opposite directions: no single flat map fixes both. The flat panels are drawn to scale within themselves.
legs3.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: one flat map on which both legs come out equal and match logged distances.
globe.title: Mirror pairs on the globe
globe.mini: Two pairs of segments, each southern one the mirror of its northern twin across the equator. On the globe, the twins are exactly equal: 4,692 km and 4,909 km.
globe.text: Two pairs of segments, each cutting across parallels and meridians, each southern segment the exact mirror of its northern twin across the equator. On the globe the twins are equal by symmetry: pair A measures 4,692 km in both hemispheres, pair B 4,909 km. The arcs look curved because on a sphere the shortest path is an arc, the great-circle route of navigation manuals [1]. Mirror symmetry across the equator is a property of the sphere that any traveller can test, by comparing a northern journey with its southern mirror.
globe.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: mirror journeys in the two hemispheres logged at different lengths.
disk.title: The same mirror pairs on two flat maps
disk.mini: The same endpoints on two flat maps, joined by straight lines. The polar disc makes a southern segment 12,383 km against 5,113 km for its mirror. The rectangular map keeps mirrors equal but stretches the pairs by 28% and 7%.
disk.text: The same endpoints plotted on the two flat maps in use, and joined by straight ruler lines, the way anyone measures a flat map [1]. On the polar azimuthal equidistant map, the flat-earth disc, each southern segment comes out far longer than its identical northern mirror: 12,383 km against 5,113 km for pair A, 8,947 km against 5,761 km for pair B. The rectangular map, latitude and longitude as a plain grid, is symmetric about the equator, so its mirrors stay equal, but it gets the lengths wrong by different amounts: 5,988 km for pair A and 5,245 km for pair B, 28% and 7% longer than on the globe. On either map the distortion differs from pair to pair, so no single correction factor can save it. On the globe, both pairs are equal twins, 4,692 km and 4,909 km.
disk.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: journeys whose logged lengths match the straight lines of either flat map better than the globe's great circles.
pairs.title: Mirror journeys: equal on the globe, wrong on both flat maps
pairs.mini: Mirror pairs of journeys, north and south of the equator. On the globe each pair is equal. The polar flat map makes one southern journey 12,383 km against 5,113 km; the rectangular map keeps twins equal but 28% too long.
pairs.text: Two pairs of journeys, each southern one the exact mirror of its northern twin across the equator. On the globe the twins are equal by symmetry: 4,692 km for pair A, 4,909 km for pair B [1]. On the polar flat-earth map, the same endpoints joined by straight lines give 12,383 km against 5,113 km for pair A and 8,947 km against 5,761 km for pair B [2]. The rectangular flat map keeps each pair equal, but at 5,988 km and 5,245 km, 28% and 7% more than the globe: no single scale fixes both. Real routes do the same: Santiago de Chile to Sydney, flown daily, is 11,369 km on the globe, 25,641 km on the disc and 15,345 km on the rectangular map [3].
pairs.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: southern journeys taking as long, at the same speed, as one of the flat maps requires.
